standard.title: Complex literary devices and intertextuality
standard.description: analyse the effect of text structures, language features and literary devices such as extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextual references
standard.prior_knowledge: Students identify and explain how literary devices create layers of meaning in texts including poetry (AC9E7LE06). They have not yet analysed the more complex devices that operate across whole texts or invoke meaning from outside the text — extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextuality.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse the effect of text structures, language features and literary devices including extended metaphor, metonymy, allegory, symbolism and intertextual references.

nodes.label: Extended metaphor and allegory
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify extended metaphor or allegory in a literary text and explain how the sustained comparison or parallel narrative generates meaning across the whole text.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify an extended metaphor or allegory in a text and explain how the extended comparison generates meaning that a single metaphor could not.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how extended metaphor or allegory structures meaning across a text — examining how the sustained vehicle shapes interpretation of individual details and the overall significance.
wider: Compare how two texts use allegory for different purposes (e.g. political critique, moral instruction, psychological exploration) and evaluate the effect of each
Examine how identifying an extended metaphor or allegorical layer changes interpretation of a text previously read as literal

response_modes.reason: Extended metaphor and allegory are easy to recognise in obvious examples (Animal Farm) but hard to identify in more subtle texts. Multiple examples across genres — prose, poetry, film — help students develop a flexible pattern for what sustained figurative layering looks like.

success_criteria: Student identifies the vehicle of the extended metaphor/allegory and the tenor it represents
Student explains how at least two details of the text derive meaning from the extended comparison
nodes.hinge_reason: Extended metaphor and allegory are the foundational devices — students who cannot identify sustained figurative layering at N1 have no basis for analysing symbolism, metonymy or intertextuality at N2 and N3, which all depend on recognising that literary meaning operates beyond the literal.

nodes.label: Symbolism and metonymy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how symbols and metonymy create meaning in literary texts by substituting part for whole, or associating object with concept.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify a symbol or metonymy in a literary text and explain the meaning it creates through association rather than direct statement.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how symbolism and metonymy operate in a range of literary texts — identifying imagery, examining examples of authors' use of devices to create meaning, and explaining the effect on audiences.
wider: Compare how the same symbol carries different meanings across cultural contexts — examining where symbolic meanings are shared and where they diverge
Analyse how a poet's use of metonymy creates compressed meaning by asking what the part stands for and what it omits

response_modes.reason: Symbols and metonymy are easiest to recognise in explicit literary examples but harder to spot in subtler texts. Encountering them across poetry, prose and visual contexts builds pattern recognition that prevents students from treating each instance as isolated rather than as a device type.

success_criteria: Student identifies a symbol or metonymic usage and names the concept or whole it represents
Student explains the specific meaning-effect the device creates — not just labels it

nodes.label: Intertextual references
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify intertextual references in literary texts and explain how they augment meaning by invoking associations from another text or tradition.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify an intertextual reference in a literary text and explain what meaning it imports from the referenced text or tradition.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how intertextual references — literary, cultural, mythological or historical — contribute to meaning in literary texts, explaining both what is imported and what effect the invocation has on the reader's interpretation.
wider: Examine how intertextual references create a two-tier reading experience — accessible to readers who recognise the reference, different for those who don't — and evaluate the implications for audiences
Analyse how a text subverts or ironises an intertextual reference, creating meaning through the gap between original and adaptation

response_modes.reason: Recognising intertextual references requires a repertoire of cultural, literary and mythological knowledge. Students with wider reading can identify more references — this is a strand where the width of prior reading directly enables the analytical work.

Intertextuality integrates all the complex device analysis — extended metaphor, allegory, symbol, metonymy can all be deployed intertextually. The final node coordinates the range of complex devices as a system of meaning-making tools that operate across texts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Intertextuality is one of the most intellectually rich areas of literary study at Y9 — the exploration of how texts generate meaning through relationship with other texts. The elaborations point to emotional responses and audience effects, making this productive territory for advancing students who enjoy making cross-text connections.
success_criteria: Student identifies an intertextual reference and names the source text or tradition being invoked
Student explains the specific meaning-effect that the intertextual reference creates in this text
